source_text: CAPUT VICESIMUM, De attributis Dei figuratis. Hactenus fuerunt attributa Dei propria: sequuntur figurata, quae per tropum de Deo praedicantur. Haec autem resolvenda et reducenda sunt ad propria, secundum regulam: Locutio impropria resolvi debet in propriam, quae illius norma est et mensura. II. Suntque alia metonymica, alia ironica, alia metaphorica, alia denique synecdochica.
english: CHAPTER TWENTY. On Gods figurative attributes.

Thus far were Gods proper attributes: there follow figurative ones, which are predicated of God by trope. But these are to be resolved and reduced to the proper, according to the rule: An improper locution ought to be resolved into a proper one, which is its norm and measure.
II. And some are metonymic, some ironic, some metaphoric, and finally some synecdochic.

source_text: III. Metonymica attributa sunt, quae de Deo per metonymiam dicuntur. Sic Deus dicitur firmitas — Psal. XVIII.2; fortitudo — Psal. XXII.20; salus et auxilium nostrum — Psal. XXVII.1,9 — quia est firmitatis, fortitudinis, salutis, auxiliique nostri auctor et dator. Sic dicitur carmen nostrum — Exod. XV.2 — quia est subjectum de quo canimus. Eodemque sensu gloria nostra — Psal. III.4; fiducia — Psal. LXV; Jerem. XVII.17; spes nostra — I Tim. I.1; Jer. XIV.8. IV. Ironica attributa sunt, quae per ironiam de Deo enunciantur. Huc referuntur Gen. III.22; I Reg. XXII.15; Job. XXXVIII.3 et XL.2; Psal.; Jer. IV.10; I Cor. I.21,25.
english: III. Metonymic attributes are those which are said of God by metonymy. Thus God is called firmness — Psalm 18:2; strength — Psalm 22:20; our salvation and help — Psalm 27:1,9 — because He is the author and giver of our firmness, strength, salvation, and help. Thus He is called our song — Exodus 15:2 — because He is the subject of which we sing. And in the same sense our glory — Psalm 3:4; trust — Psalm 65; Jeremiah 17:17; our hope — 1 Timothy 1:1; Jeremiah 14:8.
IV. Ironic attributes are those which are enunciated of God by irony. To this are referred Genesis 3:22; 1 Kings 22:15; Job 38:3 and 40:2; Psalms; Jeremiah 4:10; 1 Corinthians 1:21,25.

source_text: V. Metaphorica attributa sunt, quae Deo per metaphoram tribuuntur. Ea patres dicunt praedicari de Deo, non theologice, sed oeconomice, ut videre est apud Theodoretum dialogo secundo, qui intitulatur Inconfusus. VI. Et horum quaedam petuntur ab homine, quaedam ab aliis creaturis. VII. Ab homine petuntur, quae ab humana duntaxat natura per similitudinem de Deo dicuntur. Atque hic locum habet decantata illa loquendi ratio, quam vulgo anthropomorphosin et anthropopathian appellant, ut, cum Deo adscribuntur hominis partes, anima — Isa. I; Jer. V.9,29; Amos VI.8; membra corporis, caput — Dan. VII.9; facies — Psal. XXXI; Exod. XXXIII; oculi — Psal. XXXIV.16; II Chron. XVI.9; pupilla — Zach.; os — Job. IX; Jer.; aures — Psal.; nasus — Jer.; cervix — Jer. XVIII.17; manus — Num. XI.23; Job. XIX.21; Act. IV.28; brachium — Gen.; dextera — Psal. CXVIII.15; digitus — Exod. XXXI.18; cor — Gen. VI.6; Jer. XIX.5; viscera — Isa.; pedes — Psal.; posteriora — Exod. XXXIII; sensus interni, ut memoria — Psal.; oblivio — Psal.; externi, visus — Gen. I.4; auditus — Psal.; odoratus — Gen. VIII.21; affectus, ut laetitia — Jud. IX.13; dolor — Gen. VI.6; ira — Rom. I.18; zelus — II Reg. XIX; Isa. IX.7 — de quibus etiam vidimus supra, ubi vitam Dei ut integram expendimus.
english: V. Metaphoric attributes are those attributed to God by metaphor. The fathers say these are predicated of God not theologically but economically, as may be seen in Theodoret, second dialogue, titled Unconfused. VI. And of these some are drawn from man, some from other creatures.

VII. From man are drawn those which are said of God by likeness from human nature alone. And here that celebrated manner of speaking has place, which they commonly call anthropomorphism and anthropopathy — as when to God are ascribed mans parts: soul — Isaiah; Jeremiah 5:9,29; Amos 6:8; members of the body, head — Daniel 7:9; face — Psalm 31; Exodus 33; eyes — Psalm 34:16; 2 Chronicles 16:9; pupil — Zechariah; mouth — Job 9; Jeremiah; ears — Psalms; nose — Jeremiah; neck — Jeremiah 18:17; hands — Numbers 11:23; Job 19:21; Acts 4:28; arm — Genesis; right hand — Psalm 118:15; finger — Exodus 31:18; heart — Genesis 6:6; Jeremiah 19:5; bowels — Isaiah; feet — Psalms; hinder parts — Exodus 33; internal senses such as memory and forgetfulness — Psalms; external, sight — Genesis 1:4; hearing — Psalms; smell — Genesis 8:21; affections such as gladness — Judges 9:13; grief — Genesis 6:6; wrath — Romans 1:18; zeal — 2 Kings 19; Isaiah 9:7 — concerning which we also saw above when we treated Gods life as integral.

source_text: VIII. Quae vero ab aliis creaturis petuntur, sunt vel communia homini aliisque creaturis, vel his peculiaría. Communia sunt locus, tempus — Psal. LXVIII; XVII. Peculiaría, ut ignis — Deut. IV.24 et IX.3; Heb. XII.29; scutum — Psal.; lux — Isa.; via — Psal. LXXVII; umbra — Psal. XCI.1; ala — Deut. XXXII; sol — Psal. LXXIV. IX. Synecdochica attributa sunt, quae Deo quasi per synecdochen tribuuntur. Sic Pater Deus dicitur, non cum exclusione Filii et Spiritus sancti — Joh.; I Cor. VIII.6. Atque haec de attributis Dei, cujus perfectionis ratio consistit in negatione imperfectionum de ipso, tam proprie quam figurate dictis, de quibus observatione digna sunt quae Doctor perplexorum, Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, More Nevochim, refert: Loquitur lex secundum linguam filiorum hominum. Cujus sensus est: quicquid homines ab initio cogitationis suae intelligentia et imaginatione sua possunt assequi, id in Scriptura attribuitur Creatori. Attributa quae Deo per negationem attribuuntur sunt attributa vera; attributa affirmativa maximopere imperfecta sunt. CAPUT VIGESIMUM PRIMUM, De sacrosancta Trinitate, sequitur.
english: VIII. But those drawn from other creatures are either common to man and other creatures, or peculiar to these. Common are place, time — Psalm 68; 17. Peculiar, as fire — Deuteronomy 4:24 and 9:3; Hebrews 12:29; shield — Psalms; light — Isaiah; way — Psalm 77; shadow — Psalm 91:1; wing — Deuteronomy 32; sun — Psalm 74.
IX. Synecdochic attributes are those attributed to God as it were by synecdoche. Thus the Father is called God, not with exclusion of the Son and Holy Spirit — John; 1 Corinthians 8:6.

And these things concerning Gods attributes, whose reason of perfection consists in negation of imperfections concerning Him, said both properly and figuratively — concerning which things worthy of observation are those which the Guide of the Perplexed, Rabbi Moses ben Maimon, Moreh Nevukhim, reports: The Law speaks according to the language of the sons of men. Whose sense is: whatever men from the beginning of their thought can attain by their understanding and imagination, that in Scripture is attributed to the Creator. Attributes attributed to God by negation are true attributes; affirmative attributes are greatly imperfect. CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE, On the most holy Trinity, follows.
